questions.stem:
Statements: All cats are animals. All animals are living things.
Conclusions: I. All cats are living things.  II. Some living things are animals.
Which conclusion(s) follow?
questions.explanation: C is correct. All cats→animals→living things, so All cats are living things (I ✓). All animals are living things → some living things are animals (II ✓, conversion of universal affirmative). Both follow.

questions.stem:
Statements: No man is a tree. All birds are trees.
Conclusions: I. No man is a bird.  II. No bird is a man.
Which conclusion(s) follow?
questions.explanation: C is correct. All birds are trees + No man is a tree → No man is a bird (I ✓). I and II express the same relationship, so II also follows ✓.

questions.stem:
Statements: Some pens are books. Some books are pencils.
Conclusions: I. Some pens are pencils.  II. No pen is a pencil.
Which conclusion(s) follow?
questions.explanation: D is correct. Both premises are particular affirmatives sharing 'books' (middle term undistributed). No definite conclusion can be drawn. I and II cannot both be certain — neither is definite.

questions.stem:
Statements: All flowers are trees. Some trees are plants.
Conclusions: I. Some flowers are plants.  II. All trees are flowers.
Which conclusion(s) follow?
questions.explanation: D is correct. I: Flowers ⊆ trees, plants ∩ trees ≠ ∅ — but the overlapping trees may not be flowers, so I is not certain. II: Converse of a universal affirmative is particular ('Some trees are flowers'), not 'All trees are flowers'. Neither follows.

questions.stem:
Statements: All tables are chairs. No chair is a bed.
Conclusions: I. No table is a bed.  II. Some beds are tables.
Which conclusion follows?
questions.explanation: A is correct. All tables are chairs + No chair is a bed → No table is a bed (I ✓). II contradicts I and cannot follow.

questions.stem:
Statements: Some boys are girls. All girls are smart.
Conclusions: I. Some boys are smart.  II. All smart are girls.
Which conclusion follows?
questions.explanation: A is correct. Some boys are girls + All girls are smart → Some boys are smart (I ✓). II inverts All girls are smart to All smart are girls — converse of universal affirmative is only particular. II doesn't follow.

questions.stem:
Statements: No ring is a chain. Some chains are bangles.
Conclusions: I. No ring is a bangle.  II. Some bangles are not rings.
Which conclusion follows?
questions.explanation: B is correct. Some chains are bangles + No ring is a chain → those chain-bangles are definitely not rings → Some bangles are not rings (II ✓). I says NO ring is bangle — we can only conclude those particular chain-bangles aren't rings; there could be non-chain bangles that are rings. I is too strong.

questions.stem:
Statements: All planets are stars. Some stars are moons.
Conclusions: I. Some planets are moons.  II. All stars are planets.
Which conclusion(s) follow?
questions.explanation: D is correct. I: Planets ⊆ stars, moons ∩ stars ≠ ∅ — but the moon-stars might not overlap with the planet-stars. I is uncertain. II: Converse of 'All planets are stars' is 'Some stars are planets', not 'All stars are planets'. Neither follows.

questions.stem:
Statements: Some A are B. All B are C. No C is D.
Conclusions: I. Some A are C.  II. No B is D.  III. Some A are not D.
Which conclusion(s) follow?

options.option_text: All three — I, II and III

questions.explanation: D is correct. I: Some A are B + All B are C → Some A are C ✓. II: All B are C + No C is D → No B is D ✓. III: From I (Some A are C) + No C is D → Some A are not D ✓. All three follow.

questions.stem:
Statements: All A are B. All B are C. Some D are A. No D is E.
Conclusions: I. Some C are D.  II. Some B are D.  III. No A is E.
Which conclusion(s) follow?
questions.explanation: B is correct. I: Some D are A + All A→B→C → Some D are C → Some C are D ✓. II: Some D are A + All A are B → Some D are B → Some B are D ✓. III: No D is E + Some D are A → only 'Some A are not E'; we cannot say NO A is E (other A that are not D could still be E). III doesn't follow.
